# Native PGO and ThinLTO

Edva passes each `--cflag` argument to Clang. The LLVM IR backend
supports instrumentation PGO through `-fprofile-generate` and
`-fprofile-use=FILE`. For cross-object optimization, compile and link
with `-flto=thin` and a compatible linker. Use the Clang profile runtime,
`llvm-profdata`, and LLD from the same LLVM release. The examples below
use Linux with Clang and LLD on `PATH`. [Clang PGO](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/UsersManual.html#profile-guided-optimization) · [ThinLTO](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/ThinLTO.html)

## Instrument, train, and build

Run these commands from the compiler checkout. Use representative
training inputs and measure on separate inputs.

```bash
work=$(mktemp -d)
./edva benchmarks/server_http_router/edva.dva -O2 \
  --cflag=-fprofile-generate -o "$work/train"

LLVM_PROFILE_FILE="$work/train-%p.profraw" "$work/train" 1300000
llvm-profdata merge -o "$work/router.profdata" "$work"/train-*.profraw

./edva benchmarks/server_http_router/edva.dva -O2 \
  "--cflag=-fprofile-use=$work/router.profdata" \
  --cflag=-flto=thin --cflag=-fuse-ld=lld -o "$work/router"
"$work/router" 2850000
```

Keep the source, target, and base optimization level consistent between
training and use. Rebuild the instrumented executable and train again
when Clang reports a profile hash mismatch. A raw profile version error
during merging indicates an incompatible `llvm-profdata`. Missing
indexed profiles are diagnosed before cache lookup. Profile data can
be used without ThinLTO by omitting the last two flags.

For package builds, set these flags on the native target in
`edva.ccl` or supply them with `edva build --cflag=...` when all
selected targets are native. Edva diagnoses these native modes on
WebAssembly targets. Use an absolute profile path when building from
multiple directories.

## Separately compiled modules

Use the same Clang release for the objects and the final link.

```bash
edva worker.dva -O2 -c --module worker --cflag=-flto=thin -o worker.o
edva main.dva -O2 -c --entry --cflag=-flto=thin -o main.o
clang -O2 -flto=thin -fuse-ld=lld main.o worker.o std-objects/*.o -lm -pthread -o app
```

The last command assumes the imported standard library modules have
already been compiled to the objects in `std-objects/`.
`benchmarks/native_opt.py` runs this workflow with all the object inputs
listed explicitly. To train a modular build, use `-fprofile-generate`
on the corresponding object builds and the link, then use the merged
profile for the use builds.

The native flags keep Edva's usual foreign declarations, exported
symbols, and dynamic loader link flags. Normal linker visibility rules
still apply. Edva passes through existing debug flags. Inlining can
change which frames and variables are visible in a debugger.

## Cache behavior

Edva uses a private snapshot of the indexed profile for the build.
The cache key covers the profile bytes, ordered Clang flags, target,
Clang and linker identities, and directly named object inputs. For
instrumentation builds it also fingerprints Clang's profile runtime
archives. A replacement profile at the same path invalidates the
cached artifact. The driver keeps the usual Clang diagnostics and
treats profile mismatch warnings as errors for profile-use builds.
Advanced profile modes and backend overrides that may read files outside
these inputs bypass the cache.

## Measurements

Run `python3 benchmarks/native_opt.py --profdata /path/to/llvm-profdata`
from the checkout. The harness checks that the optimized binaries produce
the same output as the baseline on both held-out inputs. It interleaves
variants, reports the median of three uncached builds and ten measured
runs per input, and records the final executable size. Build times for
PGO use exclude the separately reported profile collection cost.

Measured on Linux x86-64 with Clang, LLD, and `llvm-profdata` 21.1.8.
The HTTP router trained on 1,300,000 requests. The separately compiled
application trained on 480,000 events.

| Workload and mode | Build ms | Bytes | First held-out ms | Second held-out ms |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Router baseline | 510 | 36,352 | 274.3 | 318.1 |
| Router PGO | 474 | 32,248 | 209.8 | 243.9 |
| Router ThinLTO | 538 | 27,208 | 272.8 | 316.1 |
| Router PGO + ThinLTO | 506 | 25,760 | 204.4 | 236.2 |
| Modular baseline | 1,568 | 180,312 | 26.0 | 30.5 |
| Modular PGO | 1,649 | 172,280 | 25.7 | 30.1 |
| Modular ThinLTO | 1,169 | 96,776 | 23.3 | 27.2 |
| Modular PGO + ThinLTO | 1,288 | 95,512 | 20.7 | 24.0 |

Held-out inputs were 2,850,000 and 3,300,001 requests for the router, and
1,200,000 and 1,410,060 events for the modular application.
Instrumenting and performing the training run plus profile merge took
562 ms and 192 ms for the router, and 1,760 ms and 22 ms for the
modular application.

PGO reduced router runtime by about 23%. ThinLTO reduced modular
runtime by about 10% and nearly halved executable size. The combined
mode reduced runtime and size on both workloads. PGO alone added
training and build cost for little modular runtime gain, and ThinLTO
alone increased router build time with little router runtime gain.
The default build remains the baseline.
